strengths: Elegant and well-motivated solution to computational bottleneck in AVS: directly predicting uncertainty maps eliminates costly iterative NeRF retraining
Impressive practical efficiency: 400× speedup in viewpoint selection with 50%+ reduction in computational resources (CPU, RAM, GPU)

Strong empirical results: consistently outperforms baselines across 8 diverse metrics (image quality, mesh quality, visual coverage) while achieving near upper-bound performance with only half the viewpoints
Effective cross-model generalization: viewpoints selected by PUN work well across different neural rendering models (NeRF and 3DGS), demonstrating robustness
Valuable dataset contribution: NUM dataset with 62,400 viewpoint-uncertainty map pairs across 13 categories with proper train/val/test splits

Comprehensive experimental validation: fair comparisons with consistent hardware, identical splits, multiple runs with standard deviations, and thorough ablations on uncertainty metrics, selection policies, and dataset composition
Good generalization to unseen object categories: strong OOD performance despite training only on 11 categories
Interpretable uncertainty maps: visualizations reveal meaningful patterns (e.g., object symmetry exploitation) that provide insights into model behavior
Well-presented paper: clear motivation (teapot example), logical flow, effective figures, and accessible writing
weaknesses: Limited scope: restricted to single isolated objects with fixed spherical viewpoint distribution; cannot handle complex scenes, multiple objects, or large-scale 3D environments

Heuristic-based uncertainty metrics: ground truth relies on image-level metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, MSE) that may not fully reflect geometric fidelity or true viewpoint informativeness; acknowledged but not addressed

Incomplete generalization analysis: while UPNet generalizes to different rendering models at test time, it is trained exclusively on Splatter-Image-generated uncertainty maps; generalization to uncertainty from other synthesis methods is unexplored

Arbitrary design choices with limited justification: redundancy threshold (0.1) and multiplicative aggregation (Eq. 2) appear ad-hoc; no theoretical analysis of potential numerical issues or parameter sensitivity beyond brief ablations
Absence of failure case analysis: only successful examples shown (Fig. 3); no discussion of failure modes, challenging scenarios, or systematic analysis of problematic object categories
Overlooked data generation cost: paper emphasizes inference efficiency but does not discuss computational expense of creating NUM dataset (training multiple view synthesis models per object)
Limited baseline comparisons: only 3 recent baselines compared; some recently proposed methods (ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER) and RL-based approaches from related work not directly compared

Narrow out-of-domain evaluation: OOD testing uses only 2 held-out categories from the same distribution; true generalization would involve different object types or alternative 3D datasets (e.g., CO3D, Objaverse)
Incremental technical novelty: UPNet is standard architecture (ViT + FC); core contribution is engineering (learning to predict rather than compute) rather than methodological innovation
Missing statistical rigor: no formal significance testing despite having standard deviations; uncertainty interpolation and aggregation lack numerical stability analysis
